A user device includes a display, a communication interface configured to communicate with a lamp having a plurality of controllable light sources, and a processor configured to execute an application. The lamp may include individually controllable light-emitting elements, such as LEDs, arranged to project a light pattern onto a target surface.

The application is configured to control the lamp to emit a source light pattern. The source light pattern defines the output of each of the controllable light sources, for example by specifying whether each light source is on or off, its brightness, its color, or another optical output characteristic. As part of the source light pattern, the application designates at least one of the controllable light sources as a marker light source. The marker light source is used to provide a recognizable reference point in the projected light pattern.

The application receives an image captured by a camera, where the image shows the light pattern as projected onto the target surface. The captured image is displayed on the display of the user device. Because of the shape or orientation of the target surface, the position of the lamp, the position of the camera, or other optical effects, the projected light pattern shown in the captured image may appear distorted relative to the original source light pattern.

The application analyzes the displayed image to detect one or more displayed locations corresponding to the intended emission locations of the marker light source or marker light sources on the target surface. These detected marker locations provide reference points that allow the application to determine how the projected light pattern is positioned, scaled, rotated, or otherwise distorted in the displayed image.

Using the detected marker locations, the application aligns a control overlay with the displayed image of the projected light pattern. The control overlay corresponds to the arrangement of the controllable light sources in the lamp and enables the user to control individual light sources by selecting locations on the displayed image. For example, when the user selects a portion of the displayed image associated with a particular light source, the application identifies the corresponding light source in the lamp and sends a control command through the communication interface to adjust that light source’s output. In this way, the marker locations allow the control overlay to be accurately registered with the camera-captured image, enabling intuitive control of individual light sources directly through the displayed image of the projected pattern.

A user device, such as a smartphone, tablet, or other computing device, runs an application configured to communicate with a controllable lamp having multiple independently controllable light sources. The lamp may include an array of LEDs or other individually addressable emitters, each capable of contributing to an overall projected illumination pattern. In use, the application establishes a communication link with the lamp, for example by wireless communication, and instructs the lamp to project a predefined source light pattern onto a target surface, such as a wall, ceiling, floor, table, or other object.

The source light pattern includes one or more marker light sources. These marker light sources are selected or driven in a recognizable manner so that their projected positions can be identified in an image captured by the user device. For example, the marker light sources may be illuminated with a particular color, intensity, modulation pattern, timing sequence, or spatial arrangement that distinguishes them from other projected light areas. The lamp then projects the source light pattern onto the target surface. Because the target surface may be tilted, curved, uneven, angled relative to the lamp, or located at a non-ideal distance, the projected pattern may appear distorted. As a result, the actual projected locations of the individual light areas on the surface may not correspond directly to their nominal positions in the lamp coordinate system or in a predefined control layout.

The user device captures an image of the target surface while the source light pattern is being displayed. This may be done using a built-in camera of the user device. The application processes the captured image to detect the projected marker light sources and determine their locations in the displayed image. The detected marker locations provide reference points that indicate how the original source light pattern has been transformed by projection onto the target surface and by the viewpoint of the camera. Based on these detected locations, the application determines a spatial mapping between the controllable light sources of the lamp and the corresponding projected light areas visible in the captured image.

Using this mapping, the application aligns a control overlay with the projected light pattern. The control overlay may be displayed on the user device screen, for example superimposed on the captured camera image or on a graphical representation of the target surface. The overlay includes selectable regions corresponding to individual light sources or groups of light sources of the lamp. Because the overlay is aligned using the detected marker locations, the selectable regions correspond accurately to the actual projected light areas, even when the projection is distorted by the geometry of the surface or the relative positions of the lamp, user device, and target.

Once the overlay has been aligned, the user can interact with it to control the illumination produced by the lamp. For example, the user may touch, drag, or otherwise select areas of the overlay to change brightness, color, saturation, beam shape, timing, or other lighting parameters for corresponding individual light sources or groups of light sources. The application translates the user’s input into control commands for the lamp using the determined spatial mapping. These commands are then transmitted to the lamp, causing the selected light sources to adjust their output in accordance with the user’s instructions.

In this way, accurate control of individual projected light areas is achieved without requiring the target surface to be flat, perpendicular to the lamp, or otherwise geometrically ideal. The detected marker locations compensate for projection distortion and enable the user interface to match the real-world projected illumination pattern. This allows intuitive and precise editing of multi-source lighting effects directly from the user device, even in environments where the projected pattern is warped, shifted, stretched, or otherwise altered by the surface and viewing geometry.

A user device is any electronic tool that allows a person to access, create, store, and exchange digital information. Common examples include smartphones, tablets, laptops, desktop computers, smartwatches, and even smart TVs. These devices play an important role in everyday life because they connect users to the internet, applications, communication platforms, and online services.

A modern user device usually includes hardware such as a processor, memory, storage, a screen, input controls, and network components like Wi-Fi or mobile connectivity. It also runs software, including an operating system and applications, which help the user perform tasks such as browsing the web, sending messages, making video calls, editing documents, or managing personal data.

Security is an important part of using a user device. Since these devices often store sensitive information, such as passwords, photos, emails, and financial details, users should protect them with strong passwords, biometric authentication, software updates, and antivirus tools when needed. It is also important to avoid suspicious links, unsafe downloads, and unsecured networks.

User devices continue to evolve with new technologies. Features such as voice assistants, high-quality cameras, cloud storage, artificial intelligence, and faster internet connections make them more powerful and convenient. Whether for work, education, entertainment, or communication, a user device has become an essential part of modern digital life.
